 Advertisement Voters overwhelmingly reject data centers in their communities on Election Day
 The tally for all ballots across the country on whether to restrict data centers was 45-1 
 Advertisement Updated: 7:34 AM PST Nov 5, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Matt Maielli Copy Editor Voters overwhelmingly reject data centers in their communities on Election Day
 The tally for all ballots across the country on whether to restrict data centers was 45-1 
 Updated: 7:34 AM PST Nov 5, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Matt Maielli Copy Editor Voters overwhelmingly rejected a variety of artificial intelligence data center projects and initiatives across the country on Tuesday at the ballot box.
 This year has seen around 50 local data center-related ballot measures across the U.S., according to Ballotpedia . On Nov. 3 alone, 47 ballot measures were set to be decided by voters on the issue of data centers.
 Advertisement Related video above: The data center debate 
 The site datacentersontheballot.com , provided by Redbud Consulting, breaks down the measures that were decided on Tuesday. To simplify often complicated ballot language, the site classifies measures as either Restrict or Allow, meaning that a measure would restrict (or ban) an AI data center or allow a data center to be built in the community. The result: 45-1.
 Facing the 47 ballot measures across the country, 45 communities voted to restrict data centers, and just one community voted to allow construction. One is still yet to be decided.
 Twenty-one of the measures were in towns and cities in Ohio alone. The next state with the most measures was Maine, with eight ballot measures.
 The measures consisted of varied language involving data center construction. Some asked about an outright ban. Some asked for a 180-day moratorium. Others asked about imposing technical limitations, such as on a site's electricity or water usage. A ballot measure in Maine asked, "Shall an ordinance entitled, 'An Ordinance to Establish a Retroactive Moratorium on Data Centers' be enacted?" An Ohio measure asked, "Shall the resolution enacting approval of a development and supply agreement term summary with EdgeConneX be approved?" And a Florida ballot asked, "Should the City Charter prohibit new data centers within the City?" The winning answers, respectively, were: Yes, No, and Yes. These all count as votes to restrict data center development.
 The measure with the highest proportion voting to restrict was in Morgan County, Illinois, with 88.3% of the 10,663 votes cast stopping data center development. The closest vote was in Sprigg Township, Adams County, Ohio, with 52.6% voting to restrict construction of data centers. On average, the pro-restriction vote percentage was over 70%.
 The lone measure that passed to allow data center construction was in Harwood, North Dakota , where the measure netted 75.6%. Notably, the ballot language seemed to be about whether to approve "additional review" of certain developments, which would include data centers, and whether to add a lengthy amendment to the city's Home Rule Charter to effect this review. 
 The opposition to data centers comes amid the Democratic Party's historic blue wave, marking a stiff rebuke of President Donald Trump and the Republican agenda, which has broadly been very positive toward AI and data centers.
 "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," the president posted to Truth Social at the end of August, saying that communities must "let data reign" in order to become "successful and rich." "The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."
